source: Fourne, Rosenbusch, Heyden, Jansen (2019) Structural and contextual approaches to ambidexterity: a meta-analysis of organizational and environmental contingencies, European Management Journal
finding: The only meta-analysis that tests structural against contextual ambidexterity head to head. Structural separation helps firms of all sizes balance exploration and exploitation. It helps more in high-technology environments.
numbers: 114 primary studies, 1991 to 2017, 33,492 organisations, moderated meta-analytic regression. Citation count 114-116.
quote: structural separation helps firms of all sizes to balance exploration and exploitation
limits: Full text blocked (repository returned a bot challenge; not bypassed). Only the abstract was read, so no coefficients, k per cell or r. The outcome is balance of exploration and exploitation, not firm performance.
agent_relevance: Gap 2 partly closed: structure favours separation, contingent on tech level. Hints that an explorer agent split from an exploiter agent may balance better than one alternating agent, but this is about balance, not results.

source: Fourne et al. (2019), same paper, service-firm finding
finding: Avoiding structural separation (the contextual route) benefits service firms. So the structural advantage is sector dependent.
numbers: Same 114 studies and 33,492 organisations. No effect size seen.
limits: Abstract only. Resources and dynamism contingencies beyond tech level and sector are not stated in the abstract.
agent_relevance: Task type may decide: interaction-heavy tasks may favour one agent switching modes, tasks with separable stages may favour split roles.

source: Wenke, Zapkau, Schwens (2021) Too small to do it all? Meta-analysis of exploration, exploitation and ambidexterity with SME performance, Journal of Business Research
finding: In small firms ambidexterity has a less positive link to performance than exploration alone or exploitation alone. Property-rights protection weakens the exploration link, and unexpectedly the exploitation link too. Authors call for research on sequential switching.
numbers: 5,488 SMEs across 34 studies. No r values in the abstract.
quote: ambidexterity has a less positive relationship with SME performance than both exploration and exploitation
limits: Abstract only. This is the Wenke line named in gap 1, but it is the SME paper, not a general meta-analysis. Effect sizes unread.
agent_relevance: Second meta-analysis (with Mathias 2014) where doing both loses to focus when resources are thin. A small token budget may mean pick one mode.

source: Junni, Sarala, Taras, Tarba (2013) Organizational ambidexterity and performance: a meta-analysis, AMP 27(4)
finding: Could not obtain pooled k, N or r. Semantic Scholar has no abstract (publisher elided it, 907 citations); the AOM page returned 403. Earlier line b04 gives only direction and moderators.
numbers: None obtained this run.
limits: Gap 1 stays open for Junni. Do not quote numbers.
agent_relevance: None until numbers are found.

source: Mathias (2014) Exploration, exploitation, ambidexterity and firm performance: a meta-analysis (Crossref abstract)
finding: Strong performance effects for exploration and exploitation each. Ambidexterity yields weaker effects than a focus on either.
numbers: 117 studies, more than 21,000 firms. Pooled r values not in the abstract.
quote: contrary to received theory, I discover ambidexterity yields weaker effects than a focus on either
limits: Abstract only; confirms x01. Mathias and Wenke 2021 agree in direction; Junni 2013 is not comparable without k and r.
agent_relevance: Weak support for a mandatory explore stage. Test focus against balance.

source: Uotila, Maula, Keil, Zahra (2009) Exploration, exploitation, and financial performance: analysis of S&P 500 corporations, SMJ 30(2)
finding: Objective archival data, not survey. The balance is a trade-off, not an interaction of orthogonal activities. The relative share of exploration has an inverted-U link to financial performance, and the peak shifts with industry R&D intensity (positive moderation).
numbers: S&P 500 firms; 806 citations. No coefficients read.
quote: inverted U-shaped relationship between the relative share of explorative orientation and financial performance
limits: Abstract only. Sample is large listed US firms.
agent_relevance: Gap 7 partly closed: an optimal explore share exists on objective data and depends on environment. Supports setting explore share by task novelty.

source: Lubatkin, Simsek, Ling, Veiga (2006) Ambidexterity and performance in small- to medium-sized firms, Journal of Management
finding: Multisource survey (CEOs and TMT members) supports that top-team behavioural integration helps ambidexterity and that ambidexterity relates to relative firm performance. Multisource design reduces the same-rater bias seen in Gibson-Birkinshaw.
numbers: 139 SMEs.
limits: Abstract only; performance is still relative and manager-reported; no effect sizes read.
agent_relevance: Gap 7 partly: a positive link survives some source separation, but not objective data.

source: Multi-Agent LLMs for Adaptive Acquisition in Bayesian Optimization (arXiv 2603.28959, 2026)
finding: Closest LLM analogue to structural ambidexterity: a strategy agent sets weights over exploitation and three exploration criteria, a separate generation agent proposes points. It beat a single LLM doing both in one prompt on hyperparameter tuning and robot pushing, but lost to EI and UCB on Rosenbrock.
numbers: llama-3.3-70b-instruct only, 30 evaluations per run, three tasks. Text gives no numbers (figures only); run count not stated.
limits: No numbers, one model, run count unknown. The split is of control from generation, not of explorer and exploiter workers. Paired-criteria ablation on robot pushing did not beat the single agent.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: first structural-vs-single LLM comparison found, but weak. The single LLM was least stable; the split gave stability.

source: LLM sequential decision making under uncertainty in biochemical domains (arXiv 2609.33061, 2026)
finding: Five frontier LLMs, three modes each. None beat the mean statistical baseline. LLMs avoid uncertainty. Reasoning models say they will explore in about 92% of traces, but stated intent has about zero correlation with realised novelty. An explicit exploration instruction did not remove the bias.
numbers: GPT-5.4, Sonnet 4.6, Kimi 2.5, Qwen3.5-397B, GLM-4.7. 7 datasets, 15 seeds per condition, 75 for statistical baselines, about 40k traces. Prior knowledge gain Spearman 0.20, one-sided p 0.03. Belief-action Pearson 0.759.
limits: Small budgets (30 to 100 points), combinatorial chemistry only; belief extraction by GPT-5-mini judges; possible memorisation.
agent_relevance: Gap 6 (generality): the explore failure appears on current frontier models and non-toy tasks, as a different failure (under-sampling uncertainty) from MACE lock-in. Telling the agent to explore is not enough; use an external rule.

source: Compute Allocation for Self-Evolving LLMs: From Depth-Breadth to Multi-Armed Bandits (arXiv 2605.29268, 2026)
finding: With C LLM calls, pure breadth (best-of-N) and pure depth (one chain) are both beaten by an interior split on some tasks. Gains over best-of-N up to +0.119, +0.102 and +0.115. Depth helps only when the model has headroom (capable model, unsaturated task).
numbers: Tasks: circle packing, min-max distance, Heilbronn triangle. Qwen3 1.7B to 14B plus Llama-3.1-8B. Budgets 8 to 512 calls. 10 seeds per cell, bootstrap 95% CI. Bilinear fit R2 0.75 to 0.92 versus 0.74 to 0.78 for budget-only.
limits: Three geometric tasks, open models only, fit is descriptive. The paper gives no clean rule for how best depth moves with budget. Circle packing favours depth, min-max distance has an interior optimum.
agent_relevance: Gap 8 partly: the best explore:exploit split depends on task and on model capability, and a small model gets no depth gain. Budget dependence not cleanly shown.

source: Compute Allocation for Self-Evolving LLMs (arXiv 2605.29268), bandit allocator results
finding: A bandit that adaptively allocates calls between arms beats fixed greedy, random and island protocols. Mean fitness is 12.3% above the strongest island baseline over 8 model-task cells. Arm pool of 5 to 20 works best; 50 dilutes refinement.
numbers: Qwen3-8B Heilbronn at C=512: greedy 0.678, ShinkaEvolve 0.738, random 0.715, UCB 0.853, EXP3.P 0.865, Thompson 0.874. Llama Heilbronn: greedy 0.254, Thompson 0.439. UCB reaches 0.95 at 92 generations vs 485 for greedy on min-max distance.
limits: Prompt confound with ShinkaEvolve noted by authors. Small gains on saturated tasks. Closed frontier models untested.
agent_relevance: Adaptive allocation beats a fixed split, which matches contextual ambidexterity more than a fixed structural split. Test adaptive explore share against fixed.

source: Holistic Diversity Management in LLM-Guided Evolutionary Search (arXiv 2610.38407, 2026)
finding: Diverse initialisation, trajectory-adaptive island selection and growth-adaptive migration give small gains. Differences are within one standard deviation for most rows. Number of islands and novelty-based sampling were not ablated.
numbers: Signal Processing, 5 seeds: no components 0.698+-0.032, diverse init only 0.703+-0.047, selection plus migration 0.700+-0.026, full 0.714+-0.022. Init: max-min 0.714, same-start 0.700, random 0.682. Island selection, 10 seeds: adaptive 0.659, uniform 0.645, UCB 0.633, round-robin 0.628. Four islands, 100 generations.
limits: Model name inconsistent in the paper; most ablations on one task; no island-count ablation. Main comparison 3 seeds.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: diverse seeding and island selection are the controls with measured effects, all small. Island count remains unablated.

source: Test-Time Scaling for Scientific Equation Discovery (arXiv 2608.28660, 2026)
finding: Best search width (parallel breadth) rises with total budget; the paper calls it a trend, not a law, and nearby widths often tie. Wider search cut runtime strongly with little quality change.
numbers: gpt-oss-20b main, Qwen3-30B-A3B check. LLM-SRBench Bio (24 tasks) and Material (25). Budgets 1 to 128 proposals. Bio width 1 to 32: runtime 7,622 s to 1,586 s, train Acc0.1 0.965 to 0.984. Three seeds.
limits: Two backbones, equation discovery only, needs an informative verifier, budget counted in proposals not tokens.
agent_relevance: Gap 8: budget does change the best breadth-depth split, so a fixed explore share is not budget neutral. Only one task family.

source: Single-Agent LLMs Outperform Multi-Agent Systems on Multi-Hop Reasoning Under Equal Thinking Token Budgets (arXiv 2604.02460, 2026)
finding: Splitting reasoning across roles (planner, parallel roles, debate, ensemble) does not beat one agent at equal thinking tokens above 500 tokens. Above 500 tokens the single agent has the best average at every budget.
numbers: FRAMES and 4-hop MuSiQue; Qwen3-30B-A3B, R1-Distill-Llama-70B, Gemini 2.5 Flash and Pro. Averages at 1k tokens: single 0.418, sequential 0.379, debate 0.388, ensemble 0.333. At 5k: single 0.427, roles 0.417, debate 0.420, ensemble 0.411. At 100 tokens debate 0.370, sequential 0.364 beat single 0.290.
limits: Multi-hop QA only. Gemini token accounting approximate. Multi-agent here is role-split, not explorer-vs-exploiter specifically. Number of questions not seen.
agent_relevance: Gaps 3 and 4 partly: role splitting at equal tokens does not help. A forced explore:exploit split is likely no better unless budget is tiny. Direct test still missing.

source: Does Multi-Agent Collaboration Pay When Agents Serve Users? (arXiv 2610.27655, 2026)
finding: Pre-registered test. A centralised multi-agent system (orchestrator, database agent, policy advisor) was worse than a single agent in 12 of 13 valid cells and tied in one. Weighted mean gain -28 points. A single agent running the same plan-and-review cycle did not differ from baseline.
numbers: About 7,950 conversations, 6 models, 3 families, 50 tasks x 3 seeds per domain. 95% CI for gain -44 to -12. Multi-agent used 2.8 to 6.1 times the tokens. Level only at 5.5x tokens. Per task better in 43 of 650 pairs, worse in 330.
limits: One architecture, one simulator; the multi-agent build had only about 25% of write orders executed as issued, below the 90% bar.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: structure by roles costs tokens and lost here; the contextual form (one agent, staged cycle) matched baseline. Supports the contextual route for interactive tasks.

source: Choi et al. (2026) MACE, models and tasks recheck (arXiv 2607.11250 v3)
finding: Lock-in shown on Qwen2.5-7B, GPT-4, GPT-5, Llama3.1-8B and Mistral-7B across a toy bandit and four QA benchmarks. The paper says seven models in four families but I could name five. In the part I read there are no per-model lock-in percentages; the earlier 50.0% to 0.0% figure was not found.
numbers: Bandit: 30 runs of T=50, pA=0.6, pB=0.5. HotpotQA 600 hard samples, Math500 L4-5, GPQA Diamond, 2Wiki 300 samples. GPT-5 picked Qwen-7B in 294 of 297 interactions.
limits: Only the first 100k characters read; appendices unread. These are the original authors, so this is breadth within one paper, not independent replication.
agent_relevance: Gap 6: breadth across families supported within one paper; independent replication absent. The 50.0% to 0.0% number is unverified this run.

source: Heuresis: Search Strategies for Autonomous AI Research Agents (arXiv 2606.25198, 2026), abstract
finding: Six strategies (greedy, MAP-Elites, Go-Explore, Islands, Curiosity, Omni) steer quality, diversity and novelty but do not expand the quality-novelty frontier. No idea rated Original. Forty fabrications confirmed in 1,628 scored runs.
numbers: 3,222 scored runs, 3 domains.
limits: Abstract summary only; no per-strategy ranking found. No island-count ablation.
agent_relevance: Diversity machinery buys spread, not better top results; require checks for fabricated results in any explore stage.

source: Island and quality-diversity LLM search papers, arXiv listing snippets (2605.30359, 2510.14150, 2604.12601, 2602.21634)
finding: Search listing only. None of nine island-using LLM search papers in the listing was found to ablate island count. CodeEvolve ablates components and matches AlphaEvolve on 5 of 9 problems.
numbers: CodeEvolve beats OpenEvolve and ShinkaEvolve on 6 of 9. Password guessing: 2.02% to 8.48% across configurations.
limits: Snippets only, not opened. Absence in a listing is weak evidence.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: island count stays an unmeasured control.

source: HTPO exploration-exploitation balanced policy optimisation (arXiv 2605.08283, 2026), listing snippet
finding: Training-time method, not a scaffold. Reports +8.6% on AIME24 and +6.7% on AIME25 over DAPO, with the gap growing with sampling budget.
numbers: Gains only as in snippet.
limits: Snippet only, not opened. RL training is outside our no-training rule.
agent_relevance: Background only; shows explore-exploit balance matters in RL, gives no scaffold evidence.

source: Search coverage note for gaps 3 and 4 (arXiv search pages, Nov 2026)
finding: Targeted arXiv searches for an explorer-vs-exploiter agent comparison, or a forced explore:exploit scaffold at equal tokens on reasoning benchmarks, found no paper. Closest are d08, d10, d14, d15. Several queries returned zero hits.
numbers: Queries: ambidextrous LLM agents, explorer exploiter, multi-agent bandit, single vs multi-agent matched compute. arXiv API and OpenAlex were rate-limited; WebSearch budget exhausted.
limits: Absence is not proof; the arXiv API and Semantic Scholar search were rate limited so coverage is partial.
agent_relevance: Gaps 3 and 4 remain open; our own experiment would be new.
